chief_complaint: acute low back pain without red flags after lifting furniture requiring evidence-based conservative reassurance and avoidance of early imaging
hpi_details: 34M accountant presents with 4 days of acute lower back pain that began the morning after helping a friend move heavy living room furniture. Describes a dull, aching soreness across his lower lumbar spine and sacrum that tightens into sharp muscle spasms when he tries to bend over or stand up quickly. Pain does not radiate down his legs. Denies tingling, numbness, weakness in feet, fever, chills, unexplained weight loss, or any changes in bowel or bladder habits (no urinary retention or incontinence).
diagnosis: Acute Non-Specific Mechanical Low Back Pain
search_text:

Disc herniation with radiculopathy (would have leg symptoms)
Cauda equina syndrome (must be excluded)
Vertebral compression fracture
Acute Non-Specific Mechanical Low Back Pain evaluation and management
Enforce the primary care Choosing Wisely clinical guideline: strictly avoid ordering routine lumbar spine imaging (X-ray, CT, or MRI) for acute low back pain (<6 weeks duration) in the absence of red flags
Memorize the clinical 'Red Flags' (TUNA FISH / Cauda Equina signs) that mandate immediate diagnostic imaging and specialist referral in low back pain: Trauma, Unexplained weight loss/Neurological deficit, Age >50 or <20 with new onset, Fever/History of IV drug use, Immune suppression, Steroid use (chronic), History of cancer, and Cauda Equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder retention or incontinence)
Prescribe evidence-based first-line conservative management combining scheduled NSAIDs (Naproxen/Ibuprofen), superficial heat application, and temporary activity modification while strictly avoiding opioid analgesics
Educate patients on the natural self-limiting recovery course (>90% resolution by 4 weeks) and explicitly counsel against prolonged bed rest, actively promoting early resumption of normal movement and core strengthening

chief_complaint: progressive memory loss, getting lost in familiar neighborhood, repeating questions, and functional cognitive decline (Alzheimer Disease Evaluation)
hpi_details: 74F retired teacher brought to clinic by her adult daughter due to a 2-year insidious progression of memory problems. Daughter reports her mother has begun asking the same questions repeatedly within 15 minutes of being answered, frequently misplaces her keys and purse inside the refrigerator or oven, and forgets the names of close grandchildren. Two weeks ago, mother got lost while driving home from her local grocery store where she has shopped for 20 years and had to be brought home by police. Mother struggled recently to pay her monthly utility bills and balance her checkbook (`instrumental activities of daily living impairment`). Mother smiles pleasantly and insists her memory is `just fine for an old lady.` Denies hallucinations, tremor, shuffling gait, or sudden step-wise drops in ability.
diagnosis: Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer's Disease
search_text:

Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer's Disease evaluation and management
Administer and interpret validated cognitive screening tools (Montreal Cognitive Assessment MoCA and Mini-Mental State Examination MMSE) to quantify objective cognitive deficits across episodic memory, executive function, and visuospatial domains
Execute the essential primary care laboratory workup to exclude reversible causes of cognitive impairment and dementia phenocopies (Serum TSH to rule out hypothyroidism, Vitamin B12 and Folate to rule out nutritional deficiency, plus treponemal/non-treponemal syphilis serology (with CSF examination if reactive) to rule out neurosyphilis, CMP for hepatic/renal encephalopathy, and structural brain MRI/CT to rule out subdural hematoma, tumors, or normal pressure hydrocephalus)
Differentiate Alzheimer Disease (insidious progressive short-term memory loss, hippocampal atrophy) from Vascular Dementia (sudden step-wise decline associated with stroke/infarcts on MRI) and Dementia with Lewy Bodies (early visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, and Parkinsonian motor rigidity)
Prescribe evidence-based pharmacotherapy: Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitors (Donepezil/Rivastigmine) for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease, reserving the addition of NMDA receptor antagonists (Memantine) for moderate-to-severe disease, and coordinate critical caregiver safety interventions (driving cessation, financial power of attorney, home safety audits)

chief_complaint: excruciating stabbing pain around left eye waking me at 2 AM every night for 3 weeks

During attacks, his left eye becomes bloodshot and pours with tears (lacrimation), his left nostril becomes blocked and runny, his left eyelid droops slightly, and his forehead sweats profusely. Unlike migraine sufferers who lie still in a dark room, during these attacks he experiences severe psychomotor agitation, pacing furiously around the living room unable to sit still or lie down. This is his third 'cluster period' in 4 years; previous episodes lasted 6 weeks and then vanished completely for over a year. Drinking a single beer instantly triggers a full-blown attack within 15 minutes.
